args.text: [lane-plover] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to a server that has moved or been retired, so pages fail or load wrongly. (2) Slow recovery: when a site switches to a backup server during an outage, cached answers delay the switch for many users. (3) Lingering bad answers: a forged or mistaken record stays in the cache longer, so harm lasts longer before it expires.

[lane-plover] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail unpredictably, so a client often cannot tell whether its first request was received. If repeating a request has the same effect as sending it once, the client can safely try again without causing duplicate payments, orders or other unwanted changes.

[lane-plover] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a universally unique identifier, version 7, which starts with a timestamp) as a primary key: (1) Larger keys: it takes 16 bytes, against 4 or 8 for a normal integer, so indexes and foreign keys grow and fewer entries fit in memory. (2) Leaked timing: because the creation time is built into the value, anyone who sees an identifier can work out roughly when the row was made. Ordering is also only approximate between servers whose clocks differ, though it still inserts far more smoothly than random UUIDv4.

[lane-plover] A write-ahead log is a record that a database writes to durable storage before it changes the main data files, so every change is safely noted first. If the system crashes, it can replay this log to recover completed changes and undo unfinished ones, keeping the data consistent.

[lane-plover] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Fair comparison: a newer client may change speed, retry behaviour or default settings, so an unpinned version could make results differ for reasons unrelated to the thing being tested. (2) Repeatability: others, or you later, can rerun the same test and get comparable figures, because the exact software used is known and recorded.

[lane-plover] Backpressure is a way for a queue to signal producers to slow down or stop when the consumers cannot keep up, so the waiting line does not grow without limit. It can work by blocking or rejecting new items once the queue is full, which protects memory and keeps delays predictable.

[lane-plover] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) a long run overlaps the next scheduled start, so two copies work at once; (2) the same schedule is installed on two servers, or a restart or clock change fires it again. One guard: take a lock before starting, for example a lock file or a database lock, and exit at once if another copy already holds it.

[lane-plover] A tombstone is a small marker that records that an item has been deleted, instead of removing the item outright. In a replicated store, it lets every copy learn about the deletion, so a copy that missed it cannot bring the old item back. Tombstones are kept for an agreed period, then cleared to save space; how long that period is depends on the system, so here it is unknown.

[lane-plover] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code, with no change between runs, and a simple rerun often clears it; (2) the failures depend on things outside the code, such as timing, test order, shared data, or the network, so they show up only now and then.

[lane-plover] A lease-based lock gives one holder the lock for a set time, and each machine decides for itself when that time is up using its own clock. If one clock runs fast or slow, the holder may think it still has the lock while the lock service thinks it has expired and hands it to someone else. Two holders then act at once, which the lock was meant to prevent. How large the skew must be to cause this is unknown.
